explanations.answer: Jesus did not first wash before the meal
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Pharisee is surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal. Jesus goes in and reclines at the table. I bet that Pharisee's eyebrows climbed his forehead, and I know a thing or two about eyebrows.

explanations.answer: Jesus did not first give thanks for the meal
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since a meal and a prayer go together so easily. But the text says nothing about thanks here. What catches the Pharisee off guard is that Jesus did not first wash. Sometimes the whole story hangs on one small detail.

explanations.answer: Jesus took the seat of honor at the meal
explanations.explanation: That's a fun picture, but the text only says Jesus reclined at the table. No seat of honor comes up at this meal. The chief seats do show up a few verses later, when Jesus talks about what the Pharisees love. The surprise at the table is that Jesus did not first wash.

Right, baker. The cup and dish are the picture, and the Pharisees are the point. Jesus says, “…but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.” He's talking about what's inside them, not what's in the kitchen cabinet.

I get why it's tempting, since He is talking about dishes. But look at where Jesus lands: “…but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.” The cup and dish are the picture. What's inside the Pharisees is the point.

That's it, friend. Jesus says they clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and wickedness. Notice the two things are put side by side. A clean outside doesn't change what's on the inside.

Fear and worry are real things people carry, but they aren't what Jesus names here. He says they are full of greed and wickedness. Jesus is describing what's inside the Pharisees, not what's bothering them.

Doubt and confusion sound like a reasonable pair, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, “…inside you are full of greed and wickedness.” The words come straight from the verse, so you can hold onto them.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…behold, everything will be clean for you.” The cup and dish were all about clean, so the word fits right in. He started with the outside, and He ends with everything.

I like ready, since it's a word I use a lot around my ovens. But Jesus doesn't say ready here. He says, “…behold, everything will be clean for you.” The whole picture of the cup and dish points to clean.

Provided sounds like a fair match for alms, since giving is about supplying someone. But Jesus says, “…behold, everything will be clean for you.” A few verses earlier He says the Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and wickedness. So the giving that comes from within is what makes everything clean, not just the outside.
That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…you disregard justice and the love of God.” They were careful about the small herbs but not about justice. That's what the woe is about.

Fasting is a fair guess, but Jesus doesn't mention it here. He says, “…you disregard justice and the love of God.” The Pharisees are careful with their tithes, down to the herbs, yet they disregard justice and the love of God. Jesus says they should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.

Sacrifice sounds like it belongs in the same neighborhood as tithes. But that isn't what Jesus says they disregard. He says, “…you disregard justice and the love of God.” They pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but justice gets skipped.

I see why it sounds that way, with Jesus saying woe to them. But He doesn't tell them to stop. He says, “You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.” The tithing stays, and justice and the love of God come too.

Right, baker. Jesus doesn't tell them to stop tithing their herbs. He says, “You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.” So the herbs stay, and justice and the love of God are added to them.

You got it, friend. Jesus says, “…you love the chief seats in the synagogues…” The chief seats are the best seats in the house. In the marketplace they love the greetings, and in the synagogue they love the best seats.

That's a good thought, but Jesus doesn't name any readings. He says, “…you love the chief seats in the synagogues…” The chief seats are what He says they love there, and the greetings in the marketplaces are the other thing on His list.

Evening prayers is a thoughtful guess, but Jesus doesn't name prayers. He says, “…you love the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.” Jesus names a seat and a greeting, and the woe is for Pharisees who love both.

That's it, baker. Jesus says they are like unmarked graves, “…which men walk over without even noticing.” Nothing marks the spot, so people pass right over. It's a hard picture, and Jesus doesn't soften it.
That would be a kind thing to do, but it isn't what Jesus describes. These graves are unmarked, so people don't know they're there. He says men walk over them “…without even noticing.”

explanations.answer: Go the long way around them
explanations.explanation: Going around makes sense when you can see a grave. But Jesus says these are unmarked graves, “…which men walk over without even noticing.” Walking over them, not going around them, is the picture He paints.

Yes, baker. The expert in the law says, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.” He heard the woes landing on the Pharisees and felt them land on himself too. He's the one who speaks up, and Jesus answers him directly.

explanations.answer: Your words are true and wise
explanations.explanation: That would've made for a calmer dinner. But the expert says nothing like that. He says, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.”

That sounds like the next thing a host might say, but the text doesn't have it. The expert says, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.” Jesus replies right then, and the talk goes on.

explanations.answer: Lift a finger to lighten the load
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says they weigh men down with heavy burdens, “…but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load.” They pile it on and don't touch it themselves. That's a heavy thing to say to anyone.

explanations.answer: Explain the reason for the rules
explanations.explanation: Explaining the rules would at least be something. But that's not what Jesus names. He says they “…will not lift a finger to lighten their load.”

explanations.answer: Pay the men who carry them
explanations.explanation: Payment isn't part of this picture. The burdens are heavy, and what Jesus says they won't do is “…lift a finger to lighten their load.” I think that's what stings about it.

explanations.answer: Witnesses consenting to their fathers' deeds
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers…” The fathers killed the prophets, and the experts build the tombs. Jesus puts those two things together.
Judges would be standing against what their fathers did, and that's not what Jesus says. He says they are “…witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers…” Consenting, not condemning.

Strangers would have nothing to do with it. But Jesus says, “…you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers…” His reason is this: “They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.” The fathers' killing and the experts' building are the two things He lines up side by side.

explanations.answer: Some will be killed and others persecuted
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. Jesus says the wisdom of God said, “…‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’” That's a heavy line, and it's worth taking slowly.

explanations.answer: Some will be welcomed and others ignored
explanations.explanation: That would be a softer ending, but it isn't what the text says. The wisdom of God said, “…‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’” It's a hard word, so I'll just say that it's hard.

explanations.answer: Some will be followed and others forgotten
explanations.explanation: Followed and forgotten sounds almost gentle. But that's not what Jesus quotes. The wisdom of God said, “…‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’”

That's right, baker. Jesus says this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets “…that has been shed since the foundation of the world…” That's a long stretch of history. He's including all of it.

I can see why it sounds like too much, but Jesus does say it. He says this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets “…that has been shed since the foundation of the world…” So it does go all the way back.

I see how it could sound that way, since they took the key. But Jesus says, “You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.” So they didn't go in themselves. They took away the key and did not enter.

That's right, baker. Jesus says the experts in the law took away the key to knowledge, then adds, “You yourselves have not entered…” They didn't go in, and they hindered others too. That makes it a double loss.
That's it, friend. Jesus says, “…you have hindered those who were entering.” People were entering, and the experts hindered them. They had not entered themselves either.
Teaching would be helping them along, and that's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says they “…have hindered those who were entering.” The experts are the ones who took away the key to knowledge.

A warning might sound like looking out for people. But Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “…you have hindered those who were entering.” To hinder someone is to get in their way, and that's what He says the experts did to people on their way in.

explanations.answer: To catch Him in something He might say
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says they were “…waiting to catch Him in something He might say.” The questions were part of that waiting. They opposed Him bitterly and kept the questions coming.

explanations.answer: To hear Him explain the Law to them
explanations.explanation: That would be a friendly reason to ask questions. But the text gives a different one. They were “…waiting to catch Him in something He might say.”

explanations.answer: To hear Him take back all the woes
explanations.explanation: That's a hopeful guess, but nothing in the text says it. Jesus doesn't take anything back here. The scribes and Pharisees were “…waiting to catch Him in something He might say.”
